articles.title: Traefik: a ForwardAuth advisory exposed my unsupported version
articles.excerpt: On October 21, Traefik published a security advisory about its ForwardAuth middleware. It is rated "high", with a score of 7.0 out of 10. I went through all my Traefik configurations to see if I was e…
articles.body: On October 21, Traefik published a security advisory about its ForwardAuth middleware. It is rated "high", with a score of 7.0 out of 10. I went through all my Traefik configurations to see if I was exposed. I am not. But while checking, I found a wider problem: my version has not received a single fix since May 2025. TL;DR : the GHSA-hrpp-p4fc-wwf8 flaw only hits Traefik setups where ForwardAuth talks to an NTLM or Negotiate authentication server. It is fixed in versions 2.11.60 and 3.7.16. Before you react to the score, read the advisory's conditions and compare them with your config. Then check the support status of your version. My setup does not use ForwardAuth. But my 3.3.7 is end of life.
articles.author: Jules Robineau

articles.title: A Website Can Be Online and Still Be Broken
articles.excerpt: Most uptime monitoring answers one question: Is the server responding? But that is not the same as asking whether the website actually works. A site can return 200 OK while the checkout is broken, Jav…
articles.body: Most uptime monitoring answers one question: Is the server responding? But that is not the same as asking whether the website actually works. A site can return 200 OK while the checkout is broken, JavaScript fails, the mobile layout collapses, or important SEO signals disappear. That gap is the reason I built Did Anything Break? Instead of treating uptime as the whole story, I wanted to look at website health from the user’s point of view. Uptime is only one layer If your server goes down, you absolutely want to know. But uptime only tells you whether the site is reachable. It does not tell you whether the site is actually usable. A more useful question is: Is the website working the way a visitor expects it to? That means looking beyond a simple HTTP response.
articles.author: Christoffer Aspelund

articles.title: I built CI for the facts in your docs (so your AI assistant stops quoting old pages)
articles.excerpt: Your AI docs assistant can give a wrong answer and cite a real page while doing it. Not because the AI is bad. Because one of your pages is out of date, and the assistant has no way to know. This post…
articles.body: Your AI docs assistant can give a wrong answer and cite a real page while doing it. Not because the AI is bad. Because one of your pages is out of date, and the assistant has no way to know. This post explains how that happens, why the usual docs checks miss it, and the open-source tool I built to catch it: TruthLayer . How a docs assistant gives a wrong answer Most "chat with your docs" assistants work like this: Split every docs page into chunks. When a question comes in, find the chunks that best match it. Send those chunks to an AI and ask it to answer, with citations. That works well, as long as every page is correct. But the same fact usually lives in many places. Say your Pro plan costs $29 per month .

articles.excerpt: On November 9, 2026, Google Cloud reported that 49% of surveyed US enterprise decision-makers said on-premises software had disrupted AI or other technology initiatives. The uncomfortable truth? A com…
articles.body: On November 9, 2026, Google Cloud reported that 49% of surveyed US enterprise decision-makers said on-premises software had disrupted AI or other technology initiatives. The uncomfortable truth? A complete rewrite may delay progress further. Make the existing system AI-ready first. AI-Ready Application Modernization: What Does It Mean? AI-ready application modernization makes existing software safely usable by AI without replacing its entire codebase. It prioritizes stable APIs, accurate and accessible data, identity-aware permissions, observable operations, and dependable tests. A legacy application becomes AI-ready when an authorized AI feature can retrieve information or execute a controlled workflow while the original system continues to enforce its business rules.

articles.title: Sec-Fetch-Site filters requests, but does not authorize users
articles.excerpt: Sec-Fetch-Site filters requests, but does not authorize users Security teams often need a cheap way to reject cross-site requests before a request reaches application code. The Sec-Fetch-Site request…
articles.body: Sec-Fetch-Site filters requests, but does not authorize users Security teams often need a cheap way to reject cross-site requests before a request reaches application code. The Sec-Fetch-Site request header provides one signal for that decision. It describes the relationship between the request initiator's origin and the requested resource's origin. A browser labels a request from another site as cross-site , while a same-origin request receives a different value. That sounds like a replacement for a CSRF token. It is not. Sec-Fetch-Site is useful defense in depth because it is generated by the browser as part of Fetch Metadata. It cannot establish who the user is, whether a session is valid, or whether a state-changing request is appropriate.
